Short case 16 · General Surgery

Oral Cavity Lesions

The one case where Bailey & Love 28e is writing directly about your patients. Oral cancer accounts for over a third of all cancers in India, and the subsite pattern here is different from the West because the carcinogen is different. Know the premalignant lesions and you have the case.

S Das: clinical method Bailey & Love: mechanism and management SRB: exam framework

1Why this case matters here, in numbers

Quote these and the examiner knows you have read the chapter B&L 28e:​B&L 53 · p.813

Two-thirds of all oral cancers occur in low-income countries, with half of those in South Asia. India has 100 000 new cases per annum.
Oral cancer is one of the most common cancers in India, with an age-adjusted incidence of 20 per 100 000, and accounts for over one-third of all cancers in India.
In contrast to western populations, cancers of the buccogingival and retromolar area account for over 40% of cancers in India and South East Asia, reflecting the commonplace use of the known carcinogens betel quid and gutka, along with smokeless tobacco.
Five-year survival is 80% for early-stage cancers but 50% overall, and in South Asia often below 50%, with a reported 5-year survival of 35% in India.

So: the disease is commoner here, it sits in a different part of the mouth here, and it does worse here. The first two facts are because of the chewing habit; the third is because of late presentation.
What counts as the oral cavity
B&L, following ICD-11: lip, gum, tongue, palate and floor of the mouth, as well as the rest of the mouth. Nasopharynx, hypopharynx and major salivary glands are excluded, and the oropharynx includes the base of the tongue.​B&L 53 · p.813 SRB: the oral cavity includes lips, buccal mucosa, alveolar margins or gingiva, retromolar area and the rest.​SRB 3 · p.356
Why the boundary mattersBecause anterior two-thirds of tongue is oral cavity and base of tongue is oropharynx, and they behave, stage and are treated differently.
Other high-incidence areas, for completeness
South East Asia, Papua New Guinea, parts of western Europe such as Portugal and France, parts of eastern Europe such as Slovakia and Hungary, and areas of Latin America such as Brazil; eastern Europe has one of the highest age-standardised rates worldwide.​B&L 53 · p.813
And the group that breaks the rules
B&L notes a rising incidence in younger patients, 45 years or younger, many of whom lack exposure to traditional risk factors.​B&L 53 · p.813 So a young non-user with an oral ulcer still needs a biopsy.

2The premalignant lesions

The full list
B&L: leukoplakia, erythroplakia, erythroleukoplakia, proliferative verrucous leukoplakia (PVL), oral submucous fibrosis, oral lichen planus and lupus erythematosus, plus the inherited conditions epidermolysis bullosa and dyskeratosis congenita.​B&L 53 · p.815
The two definitions you must get right
B&L: "A leukoplakia is a white patch or plaque that cannot be rubbed off, while an erythroplakia is a bright red velvety plaque, neither of which can" be characterised clinically or pathologically as any other recognisable condition.​B&L 53 · p.815 SRB's definition of leukoplakia matches: "a white patch in the mucosa of the oral cavity that cannot be characterised clinically or pathologically to any other disease", and it is hyperkeratotic, irreversible, persistent and adherent, and the most common premalignant lesion of the oral cavity.​SRB 3 · p.359
The two clauses that matterCannot be rubbed off, which excludes candidiasis; and cannot be given another name, which makes it a diagnosis of exclusion.
SRB's types of leukoplakia, with their risk
Homogeneous: uniform white patches, less malignant potential, the most common type, prevalent in buccal mucosa. Nodular: fine nodules on the surface, more malignant potential. Speckled: white flecks with fine nodules on an atrophic erythematous base, much higher potential for malignancy, but less common.​SRB 3 · p.359
And the features that mark a leukoplakia as dangerousSRB's list: speckled type; hard and indurated type; nodular type; presence of epithelial dysplasia; erosions and ulcerations.​SRB 3 · p.359 Those five are the answer to "which leukoplakia would you worry about?"
Which premalignant lesion carries the highest risk, and what is the transformation rate? B&L 53 p.815 names erythroleukoplakia first and gives a range of 0.13 to 34%; SRB 3 p.359 gives PVL a figure of 85%
Bailey & Love 28e
On the highest risk: "A speckled leukoplakia or erythroleukoplakia is essentially a combination of both; it carries the greatest risk for malignant change." And separately: "Among these lesions, erythroleukoplakia, PVL and dyskeratosis congenita carry the highest risk for malignant transformation." On the rate, it is candid about the uncertainty: "a review of observational studies in 2016 reported that malignant transformation in oral leukoplakia could vary from 0.13% to 34.0%", and "the natural history of these lesions remains unclear" with "an inconsistency with nomenclature internationally".​B&L 53 · p.815
SRB
Gives PVL a single figure: "Proliferative verrucous leukoplakia is rare but aggressive with 85% malignant potential; is common in elderly women; not associated with tobacco use."​SRB 3 · p.359 Note the last clause: not tobacco-related, which matters because stopping the habit will not make it safe.
Not really a contradiction: B&L and SRB name overlapping high-risk lesions, and the apparent conflict is that B&L refuses to give a single number while SRB gives one. Answer by doing both.

Say: "The highest-risk lesions are erythroleukoplakia or speckled leukoplakia, proliferative verrucous leukoplakia, and dyskeratosis congenita. Quoted transformation rates for oral leukoplakia vary enormously, from 0.13% to 34% in a 2016 review of observational studies, because the natural history is unclear and the nomenclature is inconsistent internationally. Proliferative verrucous leukoplakia is the exception, with a quoted malignant potential as high as 85%, and it is notable for occurring in elderly women and for not being tobacco-related."​B&L 53 · p.815​SRB 3 · p.359

That answer is better than either book alone, because it gives the ranking, the honest range, and the one lesion with a hard number. And it leads to the right management principle, which is B&L's: "Risk assessment forms the cornerstone of the management of these lesions", considering size, location and lifestyle exposure to known carcinogens, with biopsy advocated for accurate diagnosis.​B&L 53 · p.815 In other words: do not quote a percentage, assess the individual lesion, and biopsy it.

3Oral submucous fibrosis, which is an Indian disease

What it is, and its history
SRB: a progressive fibrosis deep to the mucosa of the oral cavity which causes trismus and ankyloglossia. The mucosa of cheek, gingivae, palate and tongue shows a mottled or marbled pallor. It is common among Asians and Indians.​SRB 3 · p.360 And the history: it was described in five Indian women from Kenya, and S.G. Joshi coined the term oral submucous fibrosis in 1953.​SRB 3 · p.360
The aetiology, with the two molecular steps
SRB: hypersensitivity to chilli, betelnut, tobacco and vitamin deficiencies probably alter collagen metabolism, leading to juxtaepithelial progressive inflammatory fibrosis of the submucosa with epithelial atrophy and dysplasia. Then the mechanism, which is the detail worth quoting: "Arecoline stimulates collagen synthesis; tannin stabilizes the collagen fibrils and makes them resistant" to degradation.​SRB 3 · p.360
SoBetel nut supplies the arecoline that lays collagen down, and the tannin that stops it being broken down. One habit, both halves of the pathology.
Why it matters twice
First, it is premalignant, and appears on B&L's list of lesions from which oral cancer can arise.​B&L 53 · p.815 Second, the trismus itself is a clinical problem: it prevents the patient eating, prevents you examining the mouth, and prevents intubation. So measure the interincisal opening and record it.

4Examination of the oral cavity

Light, gloves, gauze, and a systematic order
B&L: gauze aids the examination and intraoral palpation may be required, done gently.​B&L 52 · p.778 Inspect and then palpate, in this order: lip, labial and buccal mucosa, upper and lower gingiva and alveolus, retromolar trigone, hard palate, soft palate, anterior two-thirds of tongue, floor of mouth, then tonsil and base of tongue as oropharynx.
Describe the lesion as an ulcer
Site, size, edge, floor, base, induration, and fixity. In the mouth an everted edge with induration is a squamous carcinoma, and induration is best felt in squamous cell carcinoma.​SRB 1 · p.15 Palpate it bidigitally, particularly in the cheek and floor of mouth.
Then the things that change the stage
Trismus, which suggests deep invasion into pterygoid muscles or submucous fibrosis. Tongue mobility and ankyloglossia. Loose teeth or alveolar involvement, which suggest bone invasion. Numbness of the lip or chin, which suggests inferior alveolar nerve involvement. And fixity to bone.
And always the neck
By level, because the level predicts the subsite. Level I for lip, anterior tongue and floor of mouth; level II for the posterolateral oral cavity, tonsil and oropharynx, which is the commonest site of enlargement.​B&L 52 · p.778 Examine both sides: midline lesions of the tongue and floor of mouth drain bilaterally.

5Investigations and principles of treatment

Biopsy, always
B&L: "Biopsy of lesions is advocated for accurate" diagnosis.​B&L 53 · p.815 An incisional biopsy of the lesion including a margin of normal mucosa. In a white patch, biopsy the most suspicious part: the speckled, nodular, indurated, eroded or ulcerated area.​SRB 3 · p.359
Assess the neck
Ultrasound with guided sampling, preferring core biopsy for a node because immunohistochemistry needs tissue.​B&L 52 · p.781
Cross-sectional imaging
CT or MRI for the primary, bone invasion and the neck; and CT of the thorax if head and neck malignancy is suspected, to detect distant metastases.​B&L 52 · p.780
Risk assessment for a premalignant lesion
B&L: "Risk assessment forms the cornerstone of the management of these lesions", weighing size, location and lifestyle exposure to known carcinogens.​B&L 53 · p.815 Plus biopsy, habit cessation, and surveillance.
And the one thing that changes the population's outcome
Stopping the habit. Five-year survival is 80% in early-stage disease and 50% overall, so the gap is almost entirely about stage at presentation.​B&L 53 · p.813 India's national screening programme includes cancer of the mouth alongside breast and cervix, for all women aged 30 to 65.​B&L 58 · p.943 Mention it: it is the public health answer to the 35% survival figure.

6Rapid-fire viva

How common is oral cancer in India, and where in the mouth?

It is one of the commonest cancers in India, with an age-adjusted incidence of 20 per 100 000, accounting for over one-third of all cancers in India, and about 100 000 new cases a year. Two-thirds of the world's oral cancers occur in low-income countries, half of those in South Asia. And the subsite differs: buccogingival and retromolar cancers account for over 40% of cases in India and South East Asia, in contrast to western populations, reflecting betel quid, gutka and smokeless tobacco.​B&L 53 · p.813

What is the survival?

Eighty per cent at five years for early-stage disease, but 50% overall, and in South Asia often below 50%, with a reported five-year survival of 35% in India.​B&L 53 · p.813 The gap between 80% and 50% is stage at presentation, which is why screening and habit cessation matter more than any operative refinement.

Define leukoplakia and erythroplakia.

A leukoplakia is a white patch or plaque that cannot be rubbed off; an erythroplakia is a bright red velvety plaque; and neither can be characterised clinically or pathologically as any other recognisable condition.​B&L 53 · p.815​SRB 3 · p.359 Both are diagnoses of exclusion. "Cannot be rubbed off" is what excludes candidiasis. Leukoplakia is hyperkeratotic, irreversible, persistent and adherent, and is the commonest premalignant lesion of the oral cavity.

Name the premalignant lesions of the oral cavity.

Leukoplakia, erythroplakia, erythroleukoplakia, proliferative verrucous leukoplakia, oral submucous fibrosis, oral lichen planus and lupus erythematosus; plus the inherited conditions epidermolysis bullosa and dyskeratosis congenita.​B&L 53 · p.815

Which leukoplakia would worry you?

SRB's five features: the speckled type; a hard and indurated patch; the nodular type; the presence of epithelial dysplasia; and erosions or ulcerations.​SRB 3 · p.359 By type, homogeneous has the least malignant potential and is the commonest, prevalent in buccal mucosa; nodular more; and speckled, white flecks with fine nodules on an atrophic erythematous base, much higher, though less common. Bailey and Love agrees that speckled leukoplakia or erythroleukoplakia carries the greatest risk.​B&L 53 · p.815

What is the malignant transformation rate of leukoplakia?

Do not quote a single figure. A 2016 review of observational studies reported that malignant transformation in oral leukoplakia could vary from 0.13% to 34.0%, because the natural history remains unclear and the nomenclature is inconsistent internationally.​B&L 53 · p.815 The exception is proliferative verrucous leukoplakia, which SRB gives as rare but aggressive with 85% malignant potential, common in elderly women and notably not associated with tobacco use.​SRB 3 · p.359 Risk assessment of the individual lesion, by size, location and carcinogen exposure, with biopsy, is the cornerstone of management.

What is oral submucous fibrosis?

A progressive fibrosis deep to the oral mucosa causing trismus and ankyloglossia, with a mottled or marbled pallor of the mucosa of cheek, gingivae, palate and tongue; common among Asians and Indians. It was described in five Indian women from Kenya, and S.G. Joshi coined the term in 1953. Hypersensitivity to chilli, betel nut, tobacco and vitamin deficiencies alters collagen metabolism, producing juxtaepithelial progressive inflammatory fibrosis of the submucosa with epithelial atrophy and dysplasia.​SRB 3 · p.360 It is premalignant and appears on Bailey and Love's list.​B&L 53 · p.815

Why does betel nut cause submucous fibrosis?

Two steps from one habit. Arecoline stimulates collagen synthesis, and tannin stabilises the collagen fibrils and makes them resistant to degradation.​SRB 3 · p.360 So the nut both lays collagen down and prevents its removal, which is why the fibrosis is progressive and irreversible.

What does trismus tell you?

Either oral submucous fibrosis, or deep invasion of a carcinoma into the pterygoid muscles, which changes the stage. Either way it is a clinical problem in itself: it prevents eating, prevents adequate examination of the mouth, and makes intubation difficult. Measure and record the interincisal opening.​SRB 3 · p.360

Where does the oral cavity end and the oropharynx begin, and why does it matter?

The oral cavity, following ICD-11, is lip, gum, tongue, palate, floor of mouth and the rest of the mouth; the oropharynx includes the base of the tongue; and nasopharynx, hypopharynx and major salivary glands are excluded.​B&L 53 · p.813 It matters because the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is oral cavity while the base of tongue is oropharynx, and they differ in lymphatic drainage, in staging and in treatment, including the relevance of HPV.

Which neck level would you expect a tongue cancer to involve?

Level I for the anterior tongue and floor of mouth; level II for the posterolateral oral cavity, tonsil and oropharynx, which is the commonest site of nodal enlargement and contains the jugulodigastric node.​B&L 52 · p.778 Examine both sides, because midline tongue and floor-of-mouth lesions drain bilaterally.

A white patch in a young non-smoker. Does it still need a biopsy?

Yes. Biopsy is advocated for accurate diagnosis,​B&L 53 · p.815 and Bailey and Love notes a rising incidence of oral cancer in patients 45 years or younger, many of whom lack exposure to traditional risk factors.​B&L 53 · p.813 Absence of a habit is not reassurance, and proliferative verrucous leukoplakia is itself not tobacco-related.

Sources. S Das. A Manual on Clinical Surgery 13e (2018); Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 28e; SRB's Manual of Surgery 6e. Citations give chapter and printed page. In the 28th edition of Bailey & Love, oral cavity cancer is chapter 53. This is the chapter where the British text is most directly about Indian practice: it gives India's incidence, its survival figure, and the buccogingival subsite shift caused by betel quid and gutka. Oral submucous fibrosis and the detailed typing of leukoplakia are SRB's.
